articles.title: Jagan calls for fair elections in Srikakulam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Former Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister and YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) president Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy spoke to District Collector, Superintendent of Police and other officials, asking them to ensure free and fair elections in the Srikakulam Municipal Corporation, where polling is scheduled to be held on November 26, 2026, said former minister Dharmana Prasada Rao.

Addressing the party’s final public meeting on Tuesday evening, Mr. Prasada said that Mr. Jagan was confident of the victory of YSRCP Mayor candidate Gunda Lakshmi Devi and the corporators in 60 divisions, provided officials discharge their duties impartially, and prevent malpractices and violence.

“YSRCP leaders and activists are ready to face any eventuality on the day of the elections given the large scale violence witnessed during nominations, scrutiny, polling and counting in urban and rural local body elections. The elections in Srikakulam which are being held after a long delay, needs to be conducted in accordance to the rules and regulations. Otherwise, if the YSRCP comes to power in the 2029 Assembly elections, it will take stern action against the officials,” said Mr. Prasada.
Senior party leaders Dharmana Krishnadas, Mandavilli Ravi, Konark Srinivas and others attended the public meeting held in Srikakulam.

articles.title: Guru Nanak’s message of equality, harmony resonates at Prakash Purab
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Thousands of Sikh devotees and people from other faiths gathered at Nampally Exhibition Grounds on Tuesday to celebrate the 557th Prakash Purab of Guru Nanak Dev, the founder of Sikhism, with prayers, devotional music and a community meal.

The congregation, held on the occasion of Guru Nanak’s birth anniversary, was jointly organised by the managing committees of Gurudwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, Ashok Bazar, and Gurudwara Saheb, Secunderabad. The programme began at 11 am and continued until 4.30 pm.
Devotees offered prayers before the Sri Guru Granth Sahib, the holy scripture of Sikhism, followed by Gurbani kirtan and katha (religious discourse).

Ragi jathas (groups of devotional singers) from different parts of the country performed shabads, including Bhai Maninder Singh of Sri Darbar Sahib, Amritsar, and Bhai Kamaldeep Singh and Bhai Jagteshwar Singh of Patiala. Their renditions highlighted spiritual values and the importance of communal harmony.

Addressing the congregation, preachers recalled Guru Nanak’s teachings of belief in one God, equality irrespective of caste, creed or gender, honest living and selfless service. They said his message continue to hold relevance in a world often divided by social and religious differences.

The celebrations concluded with Guru Ka Langar, the community kitchen tradition in which devotees, irrespective of faith or social background, sat together in rows and shared a meal, reflecting Guru Nanak’s principle of equality and service.

articles.title: Wall Street roars back as Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Wall Street’s main indexes rallied sharply on Monday (November 23, 2026), led by a ​nearly 7% jump in the tech-heavy Nasdaq, as investors rushed back into AI-linked stocks ⁠after Nvidia said it had reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive.
Nvidia shares surged 32.2%, on track for their biggest one-day jump in more than two decades after an extraordinary reversal, which followed President Donald Trump’s call for Mr. Huang’s return.
Mr. Huang resigned ‌as chief executive earlier this month over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker is widely regarded as a cornerstone of the AI trade, and ‌its sharp rebound helped lift sentiment across the sector after weeks of heavy selling.

“Huang’s return ‌marks ⁠one of the biggest reversals in the history of the stock market. Never has so ⁠much value rested on the shoulders of a single executive,” said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation.
“Wall Street envisioned a stock market without his leadership and didn’t like what it saw.”
The Nasdaq-100 was on track to add more than $2 trillion ​in market value on Monday (November 23).
The Nasdaq ‌Composite and the S&P 500 were on track for their biggest one-day gains since markets surged after Mr. Trump paused his “Liberation Day” tariff package in April 2025.
Chip stocks gained, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index up 13.4% and also on track for its best session since April 2025.
The rally was broad-based in ‌the tech sphere, with the so-called Magnificent Seven stocks Tesla, Amazon , Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet climbing ​between 5.8% and 12.4%.

Neocloud and data-center companies, which came under sharp selling pressure earlier following Mr. Huang’s abrupt exit, also climbed. CoreWeave rose 21.5%, IREN gained 26.4% and Nebius advanced ⁠23.4%.
The S&P 500 information technology sector jumped 8.9% and led the gains in the benchmark index.

articles.title: Oil and gas production to pick up in 4-5 years as recent measures take effect, Petroleum Ministry says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The government expects domestic oil and gas production to pick up in the next 4-5 years as several steps taken in the recent past begin to bear fruit in an industry typically characterised by long gestation periods, The Hindu has learnt.
According to an analysis by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the current contraction in domestic oil and gas production is due to factors that took place more than a decade ago.

However, since then, the government has taken steps such as increasing drilling and exploration to record levels, changing laws and rules to provide stable terms to explorers, and opening new avenues for exploration.

“The steps taken in the last few years — new acreage, record drilling, deepwater wells and the revival of Mumbai High — will start showing up in production over the next three to four years,” the note asserted. “That is the nature of this sector: the decisions of one decade decide the output of the next.”
The note also argues that now, unlike earlier, the profits of oil and gas companies upstream companies like ONGC and Oil India are being used to fund exploration rather than subsidies.
“Until 2015, ONGC and Oil India were made to fund a large share of the subsidy on diesel, LPG and kerosene, through discounts on the crude they sold to oil marketing companies,” the note said.

According to data with the Ministry, ONGC paid ₹49,421 crore towards this subsidy in 2012-13 against a profit of ₹20,926 crore, and in 2013-14 paid ₹56,384 crore towards this subsidy against a net profit of ₹22,095 crore.

“In both years ONGC gave away more than twice what it earned,” the note said. “Money that should have gone into finding new oil and gas went into keeping retail prices down. This burden was ended from 2015-16. ONGC now keeps its earnings and has sharply raised its spending on exploration.”
According to the latest data on the Index of Core Industries, the oil and gas sectors have contracted continuously for 22 and 28 months, respectively.

“In this sector it takes five to ten years to go from awarding a block to first production,” a note prepared by the Ministry and accessed by The Hindu said. “Output in 2026 is the result of what was, and was not, done a decade ago.

“After the ninth New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP) round was launched in 2010, no new exploration round was offered until 2016,” it added. “The fields producing today were not replaced by new ones in that period, and the effect is still being felt.”

The Ministry also stated that mature oil and gas fields generally lose 7-8% of their output every year as reservoir pressure falls and that most of India’s current production comes from such fields. On the other hand, new wells, enhanced recovery, and field redevelopment are making up much of the loss.

articles.title: SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank retain D-SIB status; RBI maintains capital requirements
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has retained State Bank of India (SBI), HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank in its 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs), maintaining their respective positions under the same bucketing structure as in 2025.

Under the RBI’s framework, SBI, placed in Bucket 4, will have to maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital requirement of 0.80% of its Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs). HDFC Bank, classified under Bucket 2, will have an additional CET1 requirement of 0.40%, while ICICI Bank, placed in Bucket 1, will have to maintain 0.20%.
These additional capital requirements are over and above the Capital Conservation Buffer, strengthening the banks’ ability to absorb financial shocks and contain systemic risks.

The latest classification is based on data collected from banks as of March 31, 2026. Under the D-SIB framework, banks are categorised into different buckets according to their Systemic Importance Scores (SISs), with higher scores attracting higher additional capital requirements.

The RBI introduced the Framework for Dealing with D-SIBs on July 22, 2014, subsequently updating it on December 28, 2023. The framework requires the central bank to publicly disclose the names of designated D-SIBs annually, beginning in 2015, and assign them to appropriate buckets based on their systemic importance.

SBI and ICICI Bank were initially designated as D-SIBs in 2015 and 2016, respectively. HDFC Bank joined the list in 2017, when all three banks were identified as systemically important financial institutions.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

articles.title: Rampur’s Lavi Fair: Storytelling through 300 years of Himalayan trade and tradition
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

articles.title: Must balance ‘economic patriotism’ with cultural heritage: GJC on PM Modi’s call to stop gold purchases
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: While welcoming Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for prioritising locally-made products and reducing gold imports, the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) has said that India must balance “economic patriotism” and its cultural traditions when it comes to gold jewellery.

It argued that the sector contributes “nearly 7-8%” to the economy and supports “millions of livelihoods”. The GJC was reacting to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent and repeated appeal to all Indians to stop foreign trips and weddings, to buy local, and to only buy gold if necessary.

“The Prime Minister’s appeal for economic patriotism and greater preference for Swadeshi products is timely and welcome,” Rajesh Rokde, Chairman of the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) said.

“While we fully support the Prime Minister’s call for restraint when gold is viewed purely as bullion or an investment instrument, jewellery consumption remains closely linked to culture, craftsmanship, and livelihoods,” Mr. Rokde added.
He said that gold and jewellery hold a unique place in India’s cultural heritage, particularly during festive and wedding seasons, such as the period that India will soon enter in October-December.
“The jewellery industry, contributing nearly 7-8% to the economy and supporting millions of livelihoods, is an integral part of India’s growth story,” Mr. Rokde asserted.
‘People bought less gold, prices fell’: Modi recalls year-old appeal

“As a ₹10 lakh crore industry, the Indian jewellery sector must continue to grow responsibly, with greater transparency, value creation, and alignment with national priorities — balancing economic patriotism with India’s enduring cultural traditions,” he added.

articles.title: China announces shock corruption probe into Politburo member
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A prominent Chinese politician who is a member of the ruling Communist Party of China’s Politburo and was widely tipped for a top national leadership position in 2027 was placed under a shock disciplinary investigation on Tuesday (November 24, 2026).

The surprising announcement of “suspected severe violations” by Chen Jining, who has since 2022 been the top CPC leader in Shanghai and has served on the 25-member Politburo, left political observers in Beijing stunned.

Mr. Chen (62) was tipped to take on a prominent national role in the once-in-five-year Party Congress set for next year, which will see a major reshuffle. President Xi Jinping is expected to begin a fourth term in 2027.

Mr. Chen “is being investigated by the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Commission of Supervision for suspected severe violations of discipline and laws,” a brief statement said.

Mr. Chen was previously the president of Mr. Xi’s alma mater, Tsinghua University, and served as the mayor of Beijing between 2018 and 2022, before his promotion to the Politburo as the Party Secretary of China’s financial centre, Shanghai.

In Shanghai, Mr. Chen was popular with foreign business representatives and is among the few leaders in the top echelons of the CPC with significant international exposure, having conducted his doctoral studies in environmental engineering at Imperial College London.

Politburo members are rarely investigated, and only half a dozen Politburo-level members in the last three decades have been removed. Notably, removals have often coincided with the run-up to Party Congresses that see leadership promotions and reshuffles.

Another former Shanghai Party Secretary, Chen Liangyu, was removed in 2006, a year before the 2007 Congress that saw the anointment of Mr. Xi as former leader Hu Jintao’s successor. The year of Mr. Xi’s ascension in 2012 saw the removal of Bo Xilai, then Party Secretary in Chongqing.

Under Mr. Xi however, several Politburo-ranked members, including those from the military, have been removed. The former security chief Zhou Yongkang retired from the Politburo Standing Committee, the party’s highest body, in 2012 was placed under investigation in 2014. Another former Chongqing Party Secretary, Sun Zhengcai, was removed in 2017.

Earlier this year, PLA Generals Zhang Youxia and He Weidong were removed, along with former Xinjiang Party Secretary Ma Xingrui. Mr. Chen will be the fourth in the current Politburo to be placed under investigation, a first in China’s recent history.

Mr. Chen was present at the CPC’s Fifth Plenum in Beijing last month, a key annual meeting that confirmed the expulsion of as many as 33 members of the party’s Central Committee, including 16 PLA Generals, and concluded with a pledge to “persevere with full and rigorous party self-governance”.

articles.title: Kaliningrad: Why Russia’s Baltic exclave is a new flashpoint
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: On October 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a warning to the West. In a grand hall in Moscow, Mr. Putin sat before an audience of foreign policy experts at the Valdai Discussion Club. “If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation... then, of course, the question of the Russian Federation deploying all types of weapons at our country’s disposal will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda. This is inevitable.”

Mr. Putin continued to insist that Moscow had no plans to attack anyone — neither in 2029, not in 2030, not even in 2050. But if aggression came, he said, Russia would be compelled to respond. European citizens, he added, should understand this clearly. The warning did not appear out of nowhere. For months, NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) countries have been increasing military activities in the Baltic Sea and around Russia’s western borders.

Russia has accused the alliance of increasing military pressure around Kaliningrad and has sent a formal diplomatic note to NATO over what Moscow sees as attempts to isolate the territory. NATO, however, has rejected those accusations, saying its activities in the region are ‘defensive’.

“I can confirm that Russia sent a non-paper to NATO and that we have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” said alliance spokesperson Allison Hart. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she added.

articles.title: Estonia on the edge as Russia-NATO tensions rise
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: On October 12, NATO’s top military commander issued a stark warning to Russia. General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said that if Moscow were “foolish enough” to attack an alliance territory, NATO would destroy “anything and everything” involved in the attack.
His remarks came at a time of rising tensions between Russia and European nations. And one country that finds itself under pressure on the hot Russia-NATO border is the tiny Estonia.

When the U.S., Canada, and 10 other European nations came together in 1949, in the early phase of the Cold War, to form the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), they had a clear goal. As Lord Hastings Lionel Ismay, the alliance’s first Secretary General, famously put it, the purpose was to “keep the Soviet Union out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.”

Throughout the Cold War, NATO had been the primary military bulwark against Soviet power in Europe. After the disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia fell into a phase of strategic retreat, while NATO expanded towards Eastern Europe. This set the stage for renewed tensions once Russia started reasserting itself in the region.
The situation became even more complicated after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Brazil turns heat on Big Tech and Bolsonaro camp over foreign interference in elections
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Three weeks after President Lula da Silva’s election victory, Brazilian institutions are tightening the screws on Big Tech over alleged interference in favour of his far-right rival Flávio Bolsonaro during the campaign. The move follows Lula’s pledge to make digital regulation a priority of his government. “This election was one in which we had to overcome interference from outside through digital platforms. We are going to have to regulate them,” Lula told his supporters after winning the election on October 25.

On Saturday (November 14, 2026), the Brazilian government stepped up efforts to pass a bill which would give the country’s competition regulator (CADE) more powers to monitor the Big Tech operations. Pending since September 2025, the bill is modelled on European Union regulations and it faces opposition from Bolsonaro allies.

Meanwhile, both Big Tech and the Bolsonaro camp are feeling the heat. In a landmark ruling on November 10, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) fined Meta 7.5 million reais (US$1.5 million) for “failing to provide complete information” in a case alleging bias in the distribution of online content. The decision came after a civil society group filed a petition accusing Meta of restricting pro-Lula posts while allowing content favouring Flávio during the campaign. Meta has dismissed the allegations as “false and unfounded”, but internal documents of the company, exposed by Brazilian media, showed that Lula’s Instagram accounts had been restricted during the campaign.

In another decision that can have far-reaching consequences for Flavio and his Liberal Party (PL), a Brazilian Supreme Court judge has ordered the Federal Police (PF) to investigate possible foreign interference in the electoral process, with focus on hidden financing of campaigns. In his order, Justice Flávio Dino cited allegations that two Brazilian businessmen acted on behalf of the US-based Rockbridge Network to raise funds for Flávio’s campaign in the United States. “The prohibition on foreign financing under Brazilian law has a parallel in the US as well. For this reason, it is even more important that resources allegedly originating from that country should not be allowed to influence the Brazilian election,” the judge said in his order.

The Rockbridge Network is an American right-wing organisation co-founded in 2019 by US Vice-President JD Vance and businessman Chris Buskirk, with tech billionaire Peter Thiel bringing them together. Justice Dino has directed the police to investigate whether money and services were channelled to Flávio’s campaign. He also cited concerns over Meta’s handling of political content, including an October 22 report by the company’s Oversight Board highlighting gaps in safeguards for electoral integrity and concerns raised by United Nations observers on October 21.

articles.title: After Donald Trump’s midterm poll rout, South America breathes easy as far-right feels the heat
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: On Wednesday (November 4, 2026), rising tensions in Asuncion, the capital of Paraguay, turned violent as hundreds of thousands stormed the streets to protest locking out of their accounts in the country’s biggest bank. As fires burned and people anxiously queued outside the collapsed bank, President Santiago Pena, a former shareholder in the bank, announced his resignation.

But as Congress moved to impeach him, Mr. Pena disappeared amid rumours that he had fled to Argentina — just as Brazilian far-right leader Flávio Bolsonaro did last week before fleeing to U.S. after losing the election to President Lula da Silva. “We have information that he left the country without telling anyone. I think he went to Argentina and sought asylum,” said Paraguayan Senator Antonio Velázquez on Thursday (November 5, 2026).

Just a day after a blue wave swept across the U.S. in midterms election shaking President Donald Trump’s administration, the fall of Mr. Pena carries significance beyond the borders of the country of seven million people. Mr. Pena has been one of Mr. Trump’s closest allies in the region, having organised the first Conservative Political Action Conference last year in Asunción, where Argentinian President Javier Milei praised Paraguay’s economy as a “model” to follow.

“If the Republicans had retained the Congress, probably we would have seen Washington coming to Pena’s rescue. But the situation has changed dramatically in the U.S. and our region,” says a Brazilian diplomat, speaking strictly on condition of anonymity.

Former Argentinian President Cristina Kirchner saw it coming as she predicted on Monday (November 2, 2026) Mr. Trump’s defeat and decline of his acolytes in South America. “Paradoxically, the man who did everything he could to help right-wing leaders win elections in Latin America will lose the elections in his own country,” Ms. Kirchner told The Washington Post on November 2.

articles.title: Lula da Silva | The Pele of Brazil’s politics
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: With a smirk, Flávio Bolsonaro squinted at the camera and called President Lula da Silva “nine fingers” in the televised debate just two days before Brazil went to the polls for the presidential runoff. It was a cynical attempt to weaponise an old scar – and a gossip – against the Workers Party’s leader. Lula reacted sharply, reminding the audience how he had lost a finger on his left hand while working in a factory. “If there is anyone who lost a finger at the age of 17, it was me, working at night because I had to work,” Lula said, staring into the cameras. A red-faced Flavio didn’t know where to look. On October 25, Lula made history by becoming the first Brazilian president to finish second in the first round of an election, held on October 4, and go on to win the presidency in the run-off.

Ever since Lula entered politics more than three decades ago, his opponents have peddled the rumour that he deliberately chopped off his own finger to gain sympathy and claim compensation. But those familiar with his life know the struggles that shaped him. Born on October 27, 1945, in a dusty corner of Brazil, Lula grew up amid hunger and deprivation in the state of Pernambuco.

His family migrated to São Paulo in search of a better life, joining thousands who fled the region trapped in poverty and hopelessness. Raised by his mother, Dona Lindu, whose resilience left a lasting impression on him, Lula received only primary education before joining the workforce as a teenager. His mother passed away at 64 in 1980, while Lula was in prison during a workers’ strike. “I believe in a more just country because one day my mother taught me that, even in a simple home, no one can give up,” Lula said on Mother’s Day this year, fighting back tears as he remembered Dona Lindu.

Lula’s journey – from a parched corner of Brazil to the industrial belt of Sao Paulo – was brought to life in Lula, the Son of Brazil , a 2010 film directed by Fábio Barreto. Tracking his life, the film showed how Lula’s political training began on the factory floors of Sao Paulo’s industrial region known for its massive factories.

Amid the clutter of machines and the daily struggle with poverty, Lula rose from an apprentice to a metalworker and trade union leader and became the voice of workers who were not willing to accept low wages and political exclusion. “During the late 1970s, as Brazil’s military dictatorship sought to contain dissent, Lula emerged as one of the most prominent figures in the labour movement. His leadership brought him into direct confrontation with the regime and in 1980 he was arrested for his role in the strikes,” said Mr. Barreto.

articles.title: Indian space companies sign largest-of-its-kind deal on satellite systems
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Indian space companies GalaxEye and Bellatrix Aerospace on Tuesday (November 24, 2026) signed a multi-year contract in which Bellatrix Aerospace will supply in-space propulsion systems for the next 30 satellites GalaxEye is building.

This made the deal the “largest business-to-business order” one Indian private space company has placed with another since the space sector opened to private players in 2020, a press release noted. While private companies have participated in India’s space sector since inception, it has usually been as suppliers to the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).
The GalaxEye-Bellatrix deal was unveiled at the 5th India International Space Conclave, organised by the Indian Space Association (ISpA). The financial details of the contract were not disclosed.

GalaxEye is building the world’s first OptoSAR satellite constellation. OptoSAR is a proprietary imaging technology that allows customers to see any place on Earth through clouds, smoke, and darkness. Bellatrix builds the thrusters that steer and position satellites once they reach orbit, with hardware already flight-tested on ISRO missions.

“OptoSAR satellites are demanding customers. They need precise, repeatable orbits across a whole constellation, not a single demonstration. Our thrusters have already fired in orbit on ISRO missions, and we have built the production lines to deliver that same performance at constellation scale,” Rohan M. Ganapathy, co-founder and CEO of Bellatrix Aerospace, said in a statement. Bellatrix makes electric and green propulsion systems for satellites and orbital transfer vehicles.

Mission Drishti, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 on May 3, 2026, became the world’s first OptoSAR satellite in orbit. It validated GalaxEye’s spacecraft deployment, attitude control, onboard computing and in-house mission operations before contact was lost after a geomagnetic storm, the company stated.

In September, the Department of Science and Technology’s Technology Development Board committed ₹63.84 crore from the Government of India’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund for GalaxEye’s next multi-sensor satellite, which targets imagery sharper than 0.5 metres. Sourcing propulsion from a partner in the same city gives GalaxEye closer engineering control and shorter lead times as it builds that satellite.
“Drishti taught us that every critical system on a satellite has to be one we can see, test and improve up close,” Suyash Singh, co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, said in a statement.

ISRO chairman V. Narayanan said that private industry was now indispensable to India’s space ecosystem. “Today, we are extremely happy that 440 start-up companies are working in the space area. Whenever a launch vehicle lifts off or we place a satellite, 70-80% of the budget is pumped into the Indian industry. Without the support of Indian industry, we would not have reached the present level.”

Other officials, however, pointed out while India was putting in place a system to increase capacity, it had to work towards increasing demand for products from the private space ecosystem. “The first phase of India’s space reforms opened the sector and created an institutional framework for private participation. Now India has to work on generating heavy demand. I have less concern about capacity being created; I see a bigger need for demand to be created. The second is to have enough money coming into the sector, and number three, to have procedures at all levels. Space is not a sector that is going to give you a payback in six months or nine months. Perseverance is required, and the government must continue to have policy stability,” said Pawan Goenka, chairman, InSpace, India’s single-window regulatory and promotional body for the private space sector.

articles.title: What do lemurs and opera singers share?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Have you seen opera performers sing? You might notice how their mouths move according to how high their pitch needs to be. Imagine finding out a primate in the rainforests of Madagascar has been doing the same, possibly even before opera began?

With a pointy snout, large eyes and usually a long tail, you might have encountered this primate in one of your favourite movies, Madagascar. Remember King Julien, who loved to sing and dance? He was a type of lemur! So were Maurice and Mort, the two characters always around him.

Endemic (naturally found only in) to the island of Madagascar, lemurs are primates with diverse activity patterns, and even though they share a resemblance with other primates, they evolved independently from monkeys, apes, etc. They are considered to be the world’s most endangered mammals by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). This is mostly due to habitat loss, hunting and even unstable conservation efforts due to political and financial instabilities.

While most lemurs might survive in captivity, there are specific species like the indri which can only survive in their natural habitat, making it extremely important for us to protect the forests and their home. Today, let’s talk about this very species — the indri or babakoto!
One of the larger lemur species, the indri is the only singing lemur in the world. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement

One of the larger lemur species, the indri is the only singing lemur in the world. These black-and-white-coated primates are known for their loud, often complex, and haunting territorial songs. They often sing as duets or group choruses and even use opera-like vocal techniques to reach higher pitches. This was, in fact, a quite recent discovery.

Researchers from the University of Warwick and the University of Turin found that the world’s only singing lemur opens its mouth wider on higher notes, just like a trained soprano. The new study, published in PLOS Computational Biology , shows the first direct evidence that wild indris coordinate their mouth opening with the frequency of their songs.
The research team analysed 83 video recordings of 19 wild indris, combining field audio with markerless motion-tracking technology. | Photo Credit: Special arrangement

“The opera singers back in the day, before mics became a thing, used to tweak the shape of their mouth to sing louder and to reach farther to the audience sitting at the back. Imagine finding the same technique being used in the middle of a rainforest in Madagascar,” laughed Dr Chiara De Gregorio, corresponding author and Honorary Research Fellow at the University of Warwick.

Human singers are trained to widen their mouths as pitch rises, aligning the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract with the harmonics of the voice and amplifying the sound. For an animal communicating through a thick forest, it could make the difference between a song that carries and one that doesn’t.

“Every time the pitch of an indri’s song rose, we could see its mouth opening wider, frame by frame,” said Dr De Gregorio. “It’s the kind of fine-tuned coordination between voice and body that we usually associate with trained human singers, not with a lemur singing from the forest canopy.”

This method is called vocal tract tuning (formant or resonance tuning), and it is the deliberate adjustment of the vocal tract’s shape via the jaw, tongue, lips, larynx, and pharynx to align its resonant frequencies with the sound harmonics produced by the vocal folds.

articles.title: Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO: 6 CEOs who reclaimed their top positions
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, who had stepped down as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the chipmaker, was re-instated in the top job on November 23, 2026. Mr Huang had resigned due to an alleged Chinese spy scandal on November 12, and CFO Colette Kress was appointed as interim CEO.

The board voted unanimously to bring Mr Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately, after a series of meetings left directors satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead”, Nvidia said in a statement.
Huang’s return has put the spotlight on the ouster and return of other top bosses. Here’s a look at some of the major names.
Former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey | Photo Credit: Sandeep Saxena

The return of Mr Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia is unique, as reports suggest that senior U.S. government officials left the company’s board confident that he posed no national security risk amid concerns of China vying for the company’s advanced chips. U.S. President Donald Trump also welcomed the move as a “correct and proper decision.” I believe my ​intervention was very important to get Jensen Huang back,” Mr Trump told CNBC after Mr Huang’s reinstatement, marking an unprecedented intervention by U.S. government officials into the matters of a publicly traded company.

articles.title: Webinar on autoimmune conditions to be held on November 28
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Hindu will conduct a free health webinar on Saturday, November 28, 2026, on the topic ‘Understanding Autoimmune Conditions’. The webinar will be held from 11.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.

Autoimmune conditions occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissues and organs. These disorders can affect different parts of the body, including the joints, skin, nervous system and other organs, and may present with a wide range of symptoms.

The session will explore how autoimmune conditions develop, the role of the immune system, and the common signs and symptoms associated with these disorders. It will also discuss early warning signs, including persistent fatigue, joint pain, muscle weakness and neurological symptoms, and explain when these warrant medical attention.

The discussion will examine the challenges involved in diagnosing autoimmune conditions, the role of clinical evaluation and diagnostic tests, and the treatment options available. The panellists will also discuss long-term disease management, monitoring, and the importance of timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

Expert panellists include Aishwarya G., Consultant Rheumatologist and Clinical Immunologist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Chennai. She will discuss the immune mechanisms underlying autoimmune conditions, common rheumatological disorders, their symptoms, diagnostic approaches and current treatment options.

The panel will also feature Prabash Prabhakaran, Director and Senior Consultant – Neurology, SIMS Hospital, Vadapalani, Chennai. He will discuss autoimmune conditions affecting the nervous system, the neurological symptoms they can cause, approaches to diagnosis and treatment, and the importance of recognising neurological manifestations.
The session will be moderated by Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu .

articles.title: Bengaluru metro facilitates organ transport for second time
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: After a successful organ transport in August for the first time, Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited (BMRCL) has once again facilitated the movement of a human organ. On September 11, a live human heart arranged by Sparsh Hospital was transported via Namma Metro from Yeshwanthpur station to South End Circle station en route to Apollo Hospital.

According to BMRCL, the transport operation commenced at 11.01 p.m. and concluded at 11.21 p.m. covering seven stations in just 20 minutes. The BMRCL stated that the heart was carried inside Train ID 12, Train Set 29, accompanied by the hospital’s medical team. To ensure smooth movement, the Assistant Security Officer coordinated with the Sparsh team and metro security personnel, making special arrangements to avoid delays and provide a safe corridor for the critical transfer.
Bengaluru Metro facilitates transportation of donor heart from Goraguntepalya to Bommasandra

A live human heart arranged by Sparsh Hospital was transported via Namma Metro from Yeshwanthpur station to South End Circle station en route to Apollo Hospital on September 11, 2025. The organ was accompanied by the hospital’s medical team. | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

In August, for the first time, Namma Metro had successfully facilitated the transportation of an organ. A donated human liver, meant for transplantation, was transported from Vydehi Hospital at Whitefield to Sparsh Hospital at R.R. Nagar. The operation was executed using a combination of ambulance and metro, significantly reducing travel time during peak traffic hours.

articles.title: Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

articles.title: Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

articles.title: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: That all was not well with the Green India Mission was clear even before its approval. After the UPA-I government announced it in 2008, the Ministry of Rural Development had objected to its financial design much before the Union Cabinet approved it in 2014. But the Environment Ministry proceeded anyway and retained largely the same arrangement when it revised the Mission in 2021. Following the Comptroller and Auditor General’s report, on November 19, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) upbraided the Ministry for the Mission’s virtual failure and for still not having issued the implementation guidelines for the revised form. The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.

Together with the CAMPA, NAP, and MGNREGS funds never materialising, it is no surprise that the programmes to improve forest quality and forest cover have respectively fallen short by 91.8% and 97.5% vis-à-vis the 2014 target. The Environment Ministry had assembled a large programme around resources that it knew it could not control. Pro-climate work in practice ought to span government schemes to deliver action and justice, and the Ministry ought to have formalised the division of responsibilities and accounting system. The PAC’s new demand that the Ministry submit an implementation timetable is insufficient. From the Jal Shakti Abhiyan in 2019 to the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan in 2024, the government has often floated new programmes banking significantly on funds from existing schemes — an untenable policy when the latter also have their own obligations. And if the VB-G RAM G scheme was to also advance climate justice, the government should not have undermined the erstwhile demand-driven funding model and shifted more financial responsibility to the States. Climate action has to be timely, for which the Union government must dedicate adequate resources and proactively ensure that its initiatives are implemented.

articles.title: Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.

While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.

articles.title: Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

articles.title: National Children’s Theatre Festival concludes in Mysuru
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The National Children’s Theatre Festival, jointly organised by the Jagannath Centre for Art and Culture (JCAC) and the Indian Institute of Educational Theatre (IIET), which began on November 15, concluded on Sunday.
Speaking at the valedictory ceremony, JCAC director Ravikumar said more than nine theatre troupes from different parts of the country staged plays under the guidance of eminent directors.

He emphasised the importance of providing children with platforms to showcase their talents, stating that theatre activities at the primary school level could contribute to their intellectual development and positively influence their learning and academic performance.
He also appreciated the efforts of JCAC and IIET in promoting children’s theatre and taking Mysuru’s cultural identity to a national audience.

The plays were staged at 12 schools across the city, including Hardwicke School, Government Pre-University College in Kuvempunagar, Mathrumandali School, Bachpan Play School, Hari Vidyalaya, Mahaveer Vidya Mandir, Arivu Vidya Samsthe, BSS Vidyalaya, Morarji Desai School in Salundi, Ican International School, Learning Curve International School, and Atomic Energy School. The performances received an encouraging response.

In his introductory remarks, Indian Theatre Foundation Trustee Jayaram Patil said eight prominent theatre personalities had been invited to the festival, and nearly 2,500 children had been introduced to theatre through performances organised at the 12 schools.

The participating artists and groups included Saraswathi and B.V. Shringa from Bengaluru, Shivaram and Sundaresh Devapriya from Mysuru, Seema Ghosh from West Bengal, the Classic Theatre Foundation from Maharashtra and Ujagar Dramatic Association from Mumbai. IIET’s production, Pippi Hindu Pappu , was also staged.
Arivu Samsthe’s Janardhan and several other dignitaries were present.

articles.title: Telangana HC orders ₹2 lakh compensation to woman, 24 years after husband’s death in police encounter
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Telangana High Court has ordered the State to pay ₹2 lakh in compensation to a woman whose husband was killed in a police encounter at Chegunta in Medak district in 2001.

Pronouncing the verdict on a writ petition filed in 2002 by Ponna Venkatamma, widow of Balanarsaiah, Justice Suddala Chalapathi Rao observed that the State had failed to follow the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) guidelines and investigate the encounter. The judge held that the police authorities concerned — the Sub-Inspector of Chegunta police station, Medak Superintendent of Police and Principal Secretary (Home) — “are liable to compensate the petitioner for the loss of her husband at the hands of the police”.

On October 10, 2001, the Sub-Inspector of Chegunta police station was abducted by Naxalites during a physical confrontation at Chetla Thimmayapalli. He was released the following day. The police subsequently named Balanarsaiah among nine villagers accused of being involved in the abduction.

On December 12 that year, Balanarsaiah was killed in an encounter with a police team that included Chegunta SI Kishen Singh. The police had claimed that he was a member of the Indupriyala Local Guerrilla Squad of the outlawed People’s War Group.

Appearing for the petitioner, counsel Vasudha Nagaraj argued that the NHRC had laid down guidelines as early as 2001 for dealing with deaths in “police encounters”. Under these guidelines, the State is required to register a case involving a cognisable offence and have the incident investigated by an independent agency such as the Crime Investigation Department (CID).

The judge observed that while the State authorities had registered cases against the extremists and the petitioner’s husband, they were legally bound to register a case against the police personnel involved in the encounter as well.

The facts of the case fell within the ambit of the NHRC guidelines of 1997, which the State had failed to follow, Justice Rao noted. Despite the prescribed procedure, no investigation was conducted into the encounter, nor was any inquiry report placed before the court to establish whether Balanarsaiah’s death was the result of an act of self-defence.

However, the judge observed that directing the State to register an FIR and investigate the incident after such a long lapse of time would serve little purpose. The court, therefore, ordered the State to pay ₹2 lakh in compensation to the petitioner.

articles.title: Food poisoning: 63 tourists treated at hospital in Idukki
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Sixty-three students and teachers sought treatment from hospital after showing symptoms of food poisoning after eating from a restaurant at Kattappana in Idukki on Sunday night.
The affected group had travelled to Idukki from a coaching centre in Malappuram. They arrived in Kattappana in four buses after visiting Kodaikanal.

According to officials, the group ate mandi at a restaurant in Kattappana around 10 p.m. on Sunday. About an hour later, at 11 p.m., 52 students experienced physical discomfort and sought treatment at Kattappana Taluk Hospital, while 11 students and teachers were treated at Idukki Medical College. After receiving primary care, the group returned to Malappuram on Monday morning.

Following the incident, the Kattappana municipal health wing inspected the restaurant, though no stale food was found. Health officials collected food samples from the establishment and handed them over to the Food Safety Department for testing.

Officials noted that because the tour group had eaten at several other restaurants in Nedumkandam and nearby areas earlier, the exact source of the food poisoning can only be confirmed once test results are returned. However, some members of the group said those who consumed mayonnaise at the restaurant were the ones affected.

articles.title: No Winter Session of Parliament? Skipped only four times in history
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Winter Session of Parliament has been skipped only four times in India’s parliamentary history, and each instance was linked to exceptional circumstances, including the Emergency, the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

With the Monsoon Session yet to be prorogued, setting a record for Parliament remaining unprorogued for more than 100 days, speculation has grown over the possibility of a short special session to consider the delimitation Bill.
The absence of any move to summon Parliament for its customary winter sitting has also fuelled discussion about whether the session could be skipped altogether.

The first time Parliament missed its winter session was during the 19-month Emergency. The Lok Sabha met from July 21 to August 7, 1975, and then only from January 5 to February 6, 1976, without sitting during November or December, when the Winter Session is normally held.
The next instance came in 1979 after the premature dissolution of the Sixth Lok Sabha on August 22. The newly elected House met only in January 1980, resulting in the Winter Session being skipped.

A similar situation arose in 1984 following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on October 31. General elections were called, and the Eighth Lok Sabha held its first sitting on January 15, 1985.

After a gap of 36 years, the Winter Session was skipped again in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Amid fears over the spread of the virus and stringent social-distancing norms, Parliament did not meet after the truncated Monsoon Session that ran from September 14 to 23.
In the 12 years of the Narendra Modi government, the timing of the Winter Session has varied considerably.

On six occasions, it was convened in November; as early as November 16 in 2016 and as late as November 29 in 2021. On five occasions, it began in December, with start dates ranging from December 1 to December 15.

Article 85 of the Constitution, which deals with the summoning and prorogation of Parliament, does not prescribe the number of sessions to be held each year. It only mandates that the interval between two sessions cannot exceed six months.

The government is comfortably placed in the Rajya Sabha, where the BJP-led NDA has 151 members, compared with 64 for the INDIA bloc. According to sources, the government has also examined precedents where the Rajya Sabha was convened even when the Lok Sabha was not in session.

According to Rajya Sabha at Work , until 1961, the two Houses often commenced their sessions on different dates, except for the first session of the year or the first session after a general election.

articles.title: India, Nepal to hold 20th edition of joint military exercise Suryakiran
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: India and Nepal are set to hold the 20th edition of their joint military exercise Suryakiran, aimed at further strengthening military cooperation and deepening the defence partnership between the two neighbouring countries.

The Indian Army announced the upcoming edition in a post on X, reaffirming the enduring military ties between the two countries. “The Indian Army and the Nepali Army are set to participate in the 20th edition of Joint Military Exercise Suryakiran, reaffirming the enduring partnership between the two neighbouring nations,” the post said.
The Army also described the exercise as a reflection of the close bond between the two countries, with the tagline, “Two Nations. One Mission. An Enduring Bond.”
The announcement comes after the successful conclusion of the 19th edition of Exercise Suryakiran in December 2025 at Pithoragarh in Uttarakhand.

The 19th edition culminated with a closing ceremony following an intensive combined training cycle at the Foreign Training Node in Pithoragarh. The Directors General of Military Operations (DGMOs) of the Indian Army and the Nepal Army jointly witnessed a two-day Battalion-level Validation Exercise conducted as part of the exercise, according to the Ministry of Defence.

Exercise Suryakiran is a key bilateral military engagement between India and Nepal, providing an opportunity for the two armies to enhance interoperability, exchange operational experiences and strengthen coordination through joint training.

articles.title: Oil and gas production to pick up in 4-5 years as recent measures take effect, Petroleum Ministry says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The government expects domestic oil and gas production to pick up in the next 4-5 years as several steps taken in the recent past begin to bear fruit in an industry typically characterised by long gestation periods, The Hindu has learnt.
According to an analysis by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the current contraction in domestic oil and gas production is due to factors that took place more than a decade ago.

However, since then, the government has taken steps such as increasing drilling and exploration to record levels, changing laws and rules to provide stable terms to explorers, and opening new avenues for exploration.

“The steps taken in the last few years — new acreage, record drilling, deepwater wells and the revival of Mumbai High — will start showing up in production over the next three to four years,” the note asserted. “That is the nature of this sector: the decisions of one decade decide the output of the next.”
The note also argues that now, unlike earlier, the profits of oil and gas companies upstream companies like ONGC and Oil India are being used to fund exploration rather than subsidies.
“Until 2015, ONGC and Oil India were made to fund a large share of the subsidy on diesel, LPG and kerosene, through discounts on the crude they sold to oil marketing companies,” the note said.

According to data with the Ministry, ONGC paid ₹49,421 crore towards this subsidy in 2012-13 against a profit of ₹20,926 crore, and in 2013-14 paid ₹56,384 crore towards this subsidy against a net profit of ₹22,095 crore.

“In both years ONGC gave away more than twice what it earned,” the note said. “Money that should have gone into finding new oil and gas went into keeping retail prices down. This burden was ended from 2015-16. ONGC now keeps its earnings and has sharply raised its spending on exploration.”
According to the latest data on the Index of Core Industries, the oil and gas sectors have contracted continuously for 22 and 28 months, respectively.

“In this sector it takes five to ten years to go from awarding a block to first production,” a note prepared by the Ministry and accessed by The Hindu said. “Output in 2026 is the result of what was, and was not, done a decade ago.

“After the ninth New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP) round was launched in 2010, no new exploration round was offered until 2016,” it added. “The fields producing today were not replaced by new ones in that period, and the effect is still being felt.”

The Ministry also stated that mature oil and gas fields generally lose 7-8% of their output every year as reservoir pressure falls and that most of India’s current production comes from such fields. On the other hand, new wells, enhanced recovery, and field redevelopment are making up much of the loss.

articles.title: SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank retain D-SIB status; RBI maintains capital requirements
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has retained State Bank of India (SBI), HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank in its 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs), maintaining their respective positions under the same bucketing structure as in 2025.

Under the RBI’s framework, SBI, placed in Bucket 4, will have to maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital requirement of 0.80% of its Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs). HDFC Bank, classified under Bucket 2, will have an additional CET1 requirement of 0.40%, while ICICI Bank, placed in Bucket 1, will have to maintain 0.20%.
These additional capital requirements are over and above the Capital Conservation Buffer, strengthening the banks’ ability to absorb financial shocks and contain systemic risks.

The latest classification is based on data collected from banks as of March 31, 2026. Under the D-SIB framework, banks are categorised into different buckets according to their Systemic Importance Scores (SISs), with higher scores attracting higher additional capital requirements.

The RBI introduced the Framework for Dealing with D-SIBs on July 22, 2014, subsequently updating it on December 28, 2023. The framework requires the central bank to publicly disclose the names of designated D-SIBs annually, beginning in 2015, and assign them to appropriate buckets based on their systemic importance.

SBI and ICICI Bank were initially designated as D-SIBs in 2015 and 2016, respectively. HDFC Bank joined the list in 2017, when all three banks were identified as systemically important financial institutions.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.
